captions.instagram:
How does the liver work?

Your liver gets blood from two pipes, stores your sugar overnight, turns poison into waste and can grow back after most of it is removed. Zoom from the whole organ into its tiny hexagons and watch blood and bile flow opposite ways.

→ Your liver is the biggest organ inside you: about 1.5 kg, tucked under your right ribs.
→ It gets blood twice: three-quarters straight from your gut, a quarter fresh from the heart.
→ Zoom in: the liver is built from about 100,000 tiny hexagons called lobules.
→ Blood flows in to the middle, bile flows out to the corners, and germ-eating cells stand guard.
→ The liver is your sugar bank: it stores glucose after meals and pays it back between them.

Play with it yourself. It's free and open source: glassbox-production-fd52.up.railway.app/liverclear (link in bio)

youtubeLong.title: How does the liver work? (interactive explainer)
youtubeLong.description:
Your liver gets blood from two pipes, stores your sugar overnight, turns poison into waste and can grow back after most of it is removed. Zoom from the whole organ into its tiny hexagons and watch blood and bile flow opposite ways.

▶ Play with the interactive version: https://glassbox-production-fd52.up.railway.app/e/liverclear/
⌘ Source code (MIT): https://github.com/bdeeps/liverclear

In this video:
• Two blood supplies. The liver is the largest organ inside you, about 1.2 to 1.5 kg, under your right ribs.
• 100,000 tiny hexagons. The liver is built from 50,000 to 100,000 six-sided lobules, 1 to 2 mm across.
• The sugar bank. After meals, insulin tells the liver to store glucose as glycogen, up to about 100 g.
• Cleaning the blood. The liver turns toxic ammonia into urea for the kidneys to remove, breaks down medicines and alcohol at a roughly steady pace that no trick can speed up, and turns the pigment of old red blood cells into bilirubin, which leaves in bile.
• Bile breaks up fat. The liver makes about half a litre to a litre of bile a day.
• Regrowing and going wrong. Up to about 70% of a liver can be removed and the rest grows back to about full size in two to three months, which makes living-donor transplants possible.
